summary: This work demonstrates suppression of quasiparticle poisoning in superconducting transmon qubits to $x_{qp} = 1.88 	imes 10^{-11}$ per Cooper pair using comprehensive infrared shielding with multi-layer copper/aluminum/mu-metal enclosures and proper thermalization to the mixing plate. The quasiparticle density is inferred from parity-switching rate measurements that decrease monotonically following cooldown and reach $0.069$ Hz by day 34, while initialization errors of $	hicksim 0.01\%$ are achieved with qubits thermalized to $17$ mK.
motivation: Quasiparticle poisoning limits coherence times and error correction in superconducting qubit arrays; stray infrared radiation is a dominant controllable source, motivating systematic investigation of shielding effectiveness via parity-switching measurements.
method: Three floating transmons with $3$ GHz transition frequencies and large capacitor pads (effectively radiative antennas) were studied under three shielding configurations ranging from a dedicated light-tight multi-layer assembly to simplified designs, with parity states mapped using Ramsey sequences and analyzed via Hidden Markov Model reconstruction of noisy measurement trajectories.
result: Parity-switching rate $\Gamma_p$ suppressed from $\sim 1$–$5$ kHz (Configuration C, minimal shielding) to sub-0.1 Hz with full shielding (Configuration A), corresponding to $x_{qp} \approx 4.1 \times 10^{-11}$ on day 15 and $1.88 \times 10^{-11}$ by day 36; effective qubit temperature tracks phonon bath at $16$–$17$ mK with no saturation, confirming excellent thermalization and ruling out excess nonequilibrium quasiparticles as the dominant source of excited-state population.
